1.pericope_label: How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince’s daughter!... Thine head upon thee is like Carmel, and the hair of thine head like purple; the king is held in the galleries

schools.summary: Ellicott ties the upward order of the description to the dance named just before, since a dancer's feet draw the eye first, and quotes a verse running from the arch of the feet to the crest of the head. He corrects the fishpools to pools, our version having followed the Latin without authority, reports that the ruins of Heshbon keep the ancient name and that the Palestine exploration society had lately published a photograph of the spring-head, and notes that the margin reads crimson for Carmel from a pointing that better preserves the parallel with purple, though he prefers the mountain and allows a play on words. Delitzsch derives the title from nobility of disposition before nobility of birth, takes the article before ivory to mark a particular tower faced with ivory tablets known around Jerusalem, and explains the idiom that the head is upon her by a man's being the central unity of the members that make up his appearance, Shulamith's head ruling her form as Carmel rules the land and sea at its feet.

Gill supplies classical precedent for praising a woman by her feet, from Homer on the beautiful feet of one goddess and the golden shoes of another, and from Herodotus that an Egyptian city was assigned to the queen to keep her in shoes. On the figures that follow he reports the reading that takes not the navel but a covering for it, a jewel or plate of gold, and passes on a bishop's opinion that the clothing of wrought gold is meant, embossed with sheaves of wheat and bordered with embroidered lilies.

Clarke reads the reverse order as a fresh description, the previous chapter having gone from head to foot, and praises her walking: the richly embroidered sandals of Eastern women make the walk of a woman so shod peculiarly grand, which he thinks is why she is called a prince's daughter at once. He judges ornamental dress about the loins likely, grounding it on hundreds of decorated Asiatic drawings in his own collection, is candid that the propriety in likening the nose to a tower cannot now be discerned, and renders the closing clause of the king detained in the antechamber with his heart captivated. Wesley locates Heshbon beyond Jordan, supposes the tower a watch-tower built by Solomon on the northern border toward Damascus, and has the king unable to look away once he has seen her.
Henry applies the title wholly to the Church, a prince's daughter by new birth and by marriage, since Christ found her mean and despicable and by betrothing her made her what she is called.

debates.question: Why does the description run from the feet upward?

positions.view: Because the previous chapter had gone from head to foot, so this is a new description in reverse order, opening with praise of her richly shod walk.
Because the dance named at the end of the previous chapter would draw the eye to the dancer's feet first.

debates.question: Is Carmel the mountain or crimson?

positions.view: The mountain, though the margin's crimson better preserves the parallel with purple; a well-set head is as aptly likened to a mountain as a nose to a tower, and a play on words may be intended.
The mountain, on the idiom that the head rules the form as Carmel rules the land and sea at its feet.

outliers.note: Admits outright that the propriety in comparing the nose to a tower of Lebanon cannot now be discerned, rather than supplying a conjecture.

themes: How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince’s daughter! the joints of thy thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a cunning workman.
Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies.
Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins.
Thy neck is as a tower of ivory; thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath–rabbim: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus.
Thine head upon thee is like Carmel, and the hair of thine head like purple; the king is held in the galleries.

6.pericope_label: How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights!... I am my beloved’s, and his desire is toward me

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the exclamation as a saying of all-embracing application, nothing being more admirable than the uniting of two lives in a self-devotion that is at the same time self-enrichment; he notes that the Arabians call the palm's leaf-branches the sisters of men, hears in the next clause the vine that climbs the house wall as an emblem of the housewife, and refers the word for desire in the closing verse, from a root meaning to impel, to the sentence on the woman in Genesis. Ellicott observes that the palm's name was itself common as a woman's name, judges the supplied words for grapes an addition of the English translators, derives the term for boughs from the sound of the waving branches, and holds that the ninth verse has undergone change and is untranslatable as it stands; he also places the tenth verse as the end of a section rather than the start of one.

Gill hears the King in the galleries wonder at a beauty which could not be said how great it was. He argues from the word for stature, properly height and erectness, that tallness was reckoned agreeable in women as in men, cites the poets who likened one beauty to a plane tree and another to a cypress, and reports from Pliny that the palm's bark carries rings like steps by which easterners ascend with incredible swiftness and from Dr Shaw that the knots left by lopped boughs serve as rungs of a ladder. On the ninth verse he allows taste or breath but prefers her speech, warming and comforting in conversation.

Clarke states flatly that dates are the fruit of the palm and grow in clusters, and that these and not grapes are meant; he passes on without comment that the rubric in his old manuscript interprets the ascent of the cross of Christ, makes the wine the voice, since as good wine loosens the most backward tongue so hearing her makes the taciturn eloquent, and reads the sentence on the woman reversed, what was part of the curse being here the bride's boast, with his old manuscript rendering that she is to her love and to her the turning of him. Wesley refers the delights to the lovely features in her, thinks the palm chosen because it is constantly green and grows upward in spite of all pressures, and has the dull and sleepy made to speak.
Henry hears the church triumphing in her relation to Christ, not her own but wholly devoted to him.

debates.question: Are the clusters grapes or dates?

positions.view: Dates, since dates are the fruit of the palm and grow in clusters.
Dates, the supplied words for grapes having probably been added by the English translators to agree with the clusters of the vine following.

debates.question: What is the roof of the mouth like the best wine?

positions.view: Her speech, warming and comforting in conversation, though taste or breath are possible.
Her voice: as good wine loosens the most backward tongue, so hearing her makes the taciturn eloquent.
Undecidable as the text stands: the Greek read lips and teeth, the margin reads the ancient, and the words for my beloved are a copyist's insertion or wrongly pointed.

outliers.note: Declares the ninth verse untranslatable as it stands, where the rest translate and expound it without noticing a difficulty.
Reports the rubric of his old manuscript interpreting the ascent of the palm as the cross of Christ, without endorsing it.

themes: How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights!
This thy stature is like to a palm tree, and thy breasts to clusters of grapes.
I said, I will go up to the palm tree, I will take hold of the boughs thereof: now also thy breasts shall be as clusters of the vine, and the smell of thy nose like apples;
And the roof of thy mouth like the best wine for my beloved, that goeth down sweetly, causing the lips of those that are asleep to speak.
I am my beloved’s, and his desire is toward me.

11.pericope_label: Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field... The mandrakes give a smell, and at our gates are all manner of pleasant fruits, new and old, which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports that Hitzig opens a new scene here under the heading of Shulamith hastening home with her lover, and that on the shepherd hypothesis the bride shakes her head at the king's praise and calls to the absent shepherd, Ewald making this conceivable by supposing her lifted in spirit above the present; Delitzsch answers that nothing is more incredible than such a Shulamith. He notes that the verb for rising early is a denominative from the word for shoulder and properly means only to make oneself ready, so that the word for morning generally stands with it. Ellicott hears a reminiscence of the courtship in the woodland places, passes on the conjecture that the verse suggested a line of Milton's, gives the clause on the tender grape literally as the vine blossoms opening, glosses loves as caresses where the Greek read breasts, and derives the mandrakes as love-apples suggested by the word for loves just before.

Gill hears the church calling Christ to make good his promise, an earnest desire which grows the more it is enjoyed, and a confession that visiting the congregations would come to little unless he went with her; Christ is not unwilling, he adds, but chooses to seem so, that his people may prize his presence the more. He takes the vineyards for particular congregations, has her take the first opportunity to visit the saints and learn their condition, and reports a long disagreement over the mandrakes, some translating the word as lovely flowers, others taking it for violets, jessamine, or more probably lilies, one scholar making it branches putting forth sweet-smelling flowers, another extending that to fragrant flowers and fruits generally, and a third proposing an Arabian fruit.

Clarke stays with domestic circumstance, on the conjecture that the bridegroom rose early each morning and withdrew to the country, leaving the bride asleep with orders that she not be disturbed, so that here she asks to go with him; he keeps the country in view for observing the progress of spring, refers the mandrakes to his own note on the earlier passage, and says the literal sense here, allowing for the concealing metaphors, is of a widely different nature from what is generally given, leaving that to the reader's sagacity and prudence. Wesley has them retire from the crowd to converse more freely, finds a moral in the haste, since the church having lost her beloved by former laziness doubles her diligence, takes the vineyards for particular congregations, calls the meaning of the mandrakes much doubted, and reads the fruits new and old of the operations of the Spirit and degrees of grace in believers.

debates.question: Who is being called, and to what kind of scene?

positions.view: Not a shepherd lover: the scene-change proposed for this verse, and the bride's supposed refusal of the king, are incredible.
A husband withdrawing daily to the country, whom the bride here asks to accompany.
Christ, called by the church to go with her as she visits the congregations.
A reminiscence of the courtship in the woodland places named earlier in the book.
Undetermined: violets, jessamine, lilies, sweet-smelling branches, or an Arabian fruit have all been proposed.
Sweet and pleasant flowers; if mandrakes, of another sort than ours, since flowers of one kind differ across climates.
Love-apples, the name suggested by the word for loves just before and by the qualities ascribed to the plant.

outliers.note: Hints that the literal sense of the closing verse, allowing for the concealing metaphors, is widely different from what is generally given, but declines to state it and leaves it to the reader's prudence.

themes: Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field; let us lodge in the villages.
Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see if the vine flourish, whether the tender grape appear, and the pomegranates bud forth: there will I give thee my loves.
The mandrakes give a smell, and at our gates are all manner of pleasant fruits, new and old, which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved.
